prompt: In Go 1.27.1, how does a new goroutine's stack begin, and what happens when a call needs more room than it has?
hint: Compare the two numbers the section put side by side: `ulimit -s` and `stackMin`.

choices.text: It starts at 2,048 bytes and is copied whole to a block twice the size
choices.why: Right. `stackMin = 2048` in `stack.go`, and growth is a copy to a doubled block; `~/mem-stacks` watched `main`'s stack reach about 32 MiB that way.

choices.text: It starts at 8 MiB, like a thread, and the program dies past that
choices.why: 8,192 KiB is what `ulimit -s` printed for the main thread. A goroutine starts four thousand times smaller and grows.

choices.text: It starts at 2 KiB, and further frames are put on the heap
choices.why: Frames never move to the heap. The whole stack is moved to a bigger block, which is why `x` changed address.

choices.text: It starts at 2 KiB and gains a linked second segment
choices.why: Linked segments are not what 1.27.1 does: `copystack` allocates one new block, copies the used part and frees the old one.

prompt: In `~/mem-stacks`, the local variable `x` printed one address before `down(100000)` and another after it, although no line of the program assigned it again. Why?
hint: `x` stayed in `main`'s frame the whole time.

choices.text: `down` overwrote `x` with a copy of itself
choices.why: `down` never sees `x`: it has its own frames with its own `pad` arrays. The value of `x` is unchanged; only where it sits changed.

choices.text: The deep call made `x` escape to the heap
choices.why: Escape is decided by the compiler when it builds the program, not during a run. `uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&x))` keeps `x` in the frame.

choices.text: Growing the stack copied every frame, `x`'s too
choices.why: Right. Growth copies the whole stack to a new block, so every frame on it, and every variable in each frame, has a new address afterwards. The collections that shrank it moved `x` again.

choices.text: The collector compacted the stack to close gaps between frames
choices.why: The collector did shrink the stack later, by copying it to a block half the size. The first move happened during `down`, before any collection, because the stack had run out.

prompt: Go's heap collector never moves a value to a new address, yet the runtime moves whole goroutine stacks freely. What makes the stack the easy case?
hint: Think about where a pointer to something on a stack is allowed to live.

choices.text: Stacks are small enough to copy within one stop of the world
choices.why: Stacks are copied by their own goroutine, with nothing stopped, and one in `~/mem-stacks` reached about 32 MiB. Size is not what makes it safe.

choices.text: No heap value is allowed to point into a stack, so only the stack's own pointers need fixing
choices.why: Right. It is the first invariant of escape analysis: anything whose address would be stored on the heap is put on the heap itself. The runtime adjusts pointers inside the copied stack and has nothing else to search.

choices.text: Stack values hold no pointers, so a copy is a plain `memmove`
choices.why: Frames hold pointers all the time, and the compiler records which words do so that the copy can adjust them.

choices.text: The old stack stays mapped, so stale pointers still read the right data
choices.why: The old block is freed after the copy. A stale pointer into it would read whatever came next, which is why the design needs no such pointers.

prompt: In `~/mem-stacks`, 10,000 waiting goroutines took 20,000 KiB of stack. At the same starting size, how many KiB would 250,000 waiting goroutines take?
hint: Work out the size of one stack first.

prompt: In the collector's three colours, what does a grey value mean?
hint: One of the three is the marker's to-do list.

choices.text: Reached, its pointers not yet followed
choices.why: Right. Grey values are the work left: the marker takes one, shades what it points at and turns it black. Marking ends when nothing is grey.

choices.text: Not reached yet, and garbage if it stays so
choices.why: That is white. White at the end of marking is what the sweep reuses.

choices.text: Reached, with every pointer inside it already followed
choices.why: That is black. The marker will not look inside a black value again, which is exactly why the write barrier exists.

choices.text: Allocated during the cycle, kept until the next one
choices.why: Values allocated while marking runs are made black at once, by `mgc.go`'s own description.

prompt: While a cycle is marking, the program runs `a.next = c` and then `b.next = nil`, where `a` is black, `b` is grey and `b.next` was the only pointer to `c`. Which part of the write barrier keeps `c` alive?
hint: Look at which value each `shade` call receives, in the five lines from `mbarrier.go`.

choices.text: `shade(ptr)` in `b.next = nil`, which colours the new value
choices.why: The new value there is `nil`, and there is nothing to colour. The old value is the one in danger.

choices.text: `shade(*slot)` in `b.next = nil`, colouring `c` on its way out
choices.why: Right. The deletion half of the barrier shades what the field pointed at before the write, so removing the last grey path to `c` turns `c` grey instead of leaving it white.

choices.text: No barrier is involved, because `a` is black and is rescanned at the end
choices.why: Black values are not rescanned. Without the barrier `c` would stay white, be swept and be freed while `a` still points at it.

choices.text: Mark termination stops the world and checks every black value for white pointers
choices.why: Mark termination is a brief stop for housekeeping; in the trace it lasted 0.004 ms. It does not walk the heap again.

prompt: Match each piece of this `gctrace` line from `hits count` to what it reports: `gc 2 @0.017s 1%: 0.032+1.2+0.004 ms clock, 0.13+0.025/0.001/0.11+0.019 ms cpu, 3->3->0 MB, 4 MB goal, 0 MB stacks, 0 MB globals, 4 P`.
hint: The documentation's format is in `go doc runtime`, under `gctrace`.

pairs.right: the stop that starts the cycle, in wall-clock time
marking, while the program kept running
marking by assists, the background worker and idle processors
the heap at the start and end of marking, and what survived
the heap size the cycle meant to finish under

right_distractors: the time since the previous collection ended

prompt: Every line of the `hits count` trace says `3->3->0 MB, 4 MB goal`. With nothing surviving and `GOGC=100`, why is the goal 4 MB and not twice nothing?
hint: Section 03 ran the same program under `GOGC=50` and `GOGC=200` and read the fifth line.

choices.text: The goal counts the binary's own size, about 4 MB
choices.why: The binary was not counted anywhere in the goal formula. And `GOGC=200` printed an 8 MB goal for the same binary.

choices.text: The pacer has a floor, 4 MB scaled by `GOGC` over 100
choices.why: Right. `defaultHeapMinimum` is 4 MB at `GOGC=100`, and `heapMinimum = defaultHeapMinimum * GOGC / 100`; the other runs printed goals of 2 MB and 8 MB.

choices.text: Four processors each reserve 1 MB of heap for their caches
choices.why: The `4 P` at the end is a coincidence here: under `GOGC=50` the same four processors gave a 2 MB goal.

choices.text: `0 MB` is rounded down, and the live heap was really 2 MB
choices.why: Rounding would not double anything in a stable way, and the goal moved with `GOGC` exactly in proportion: 2, 4, 8.

prompt: `gc 14` of `slowest` found 92 MB alive, with 0 MB of stacks and globals. If the program had run with `GOGC=50`, what heap goal, in MB, would the next cycle have aimed for?
hint: The line of `mgcpacer.go`: the marked heap, plus the marked heap, stacks and globals times `GOGC` over 100.

prompt: Under `GOMEMLIMIT=100MiB`, `slowest` ran 66 collections in 3.13 s, and its trace showed `161->164->162 MB, 161 MB goal` with the next cycle 48 ms later. What was going on?
hint: Compare the three heap numbers with each other, and the goal with all three.

choices.text: The live heap was over the limit; each cycle freed almost nothing
choices.why: Right. 162 of 164 MB survived, the heap was already past 100 MiB, and the goal stayed pinned to the heap as it stood: the start of a death spiral, held back by the limiter.

choices.text: The program leaked memory, which the limit exposed
choices.why: Every value it kept, it used: the entries it sorts. Nothing was unreachable and kept; the limit was simply below what the program needs.

choices.text: The limit made the runtime return memory to Linux after every cycle
choices.why: Returning memory does not explain a heap that stays at 162 MB alive. The collections themselves are the cost.

choices.text: The runtime stopped the world for each of those 66 collections
choices.why: The stops in those lines lasted under a millisecond; the marking ran beside the program. It was the sheer number of cycles that cost the time.

prompt: Which of these are true of `GOMEMLIMIT` in Go 1.27.1? Choose every one that applies.
hint: Remember the run with `GOGC=off GOMEMLIMIT=400MiB` and what `cgroup_linux.go` reads.

choices.text: It is soft: memory the program still uses is kept even past the limit
choices.why: Right. The 400 MiB run peaked at 453 MiB, and nothing failed. The limit makes the runtime collect harder; it cannot free a reachable byte.

choices.text: The runtime does not read it from a container; it has to be set
choices.why: Right. The runtime's control-group code reads the processor quota for `GOMAXPROCS` and nothing about memory.

choices.text: With `GOGC=off` it is the only thing that starts a collection
choices.why: Right. `GOGC=off` removes the proportional rule, and the limit is still respected; that run needed three collections in all.

choices.text: It counts the binary and memory that C code allocates
choices.why: `SetMemoryLimit`'s documentation names both as excluded, which is one reason a container needs a margin below its real limit.

choices.text: Going over it ends the program with an out-of-memory error
choices.why: The 100 MiB run went far past the limit and finished, slowly. The kernel may kill a process over its container's limit; the runtime does not.

prompt: With `GOGC=off`, `slowest` used 0.74 s of user time instead of 1.26 s, yet its wall-clock time fell only from 1.61 s to 1.39 s. On a server whose four processors are already busy, what would you expect the same change to do?
hint: Ask where the 0.5 s of marking had been running in the lab.

choices.text: Nothing different: wall-clock time is what users see, and it barely moved
choices.why: It barely moved in the lab because the marking used processors that were otherwise idle. On a busy server those processors are doing other work.

choices.text: Save more wall-clock time than in the lab, and cost far more memory
choices.why: Right. The 0.5 s of marking would have been taken from other work, so removing it gains more there; the peak still doubles toward everything ever allocated, about 1 GB here.

choices.text: Make the program slower, because the heap would never be compacted
choices.why: Go's collector never compacts, on or off. What `off` changes is that nothing is reused.

choices.text: Lower the peak memory, since no cycle leaves garbage half swept
choices.why: With no collection, every byte ever allocated stays: the lab's peak went from about 0.6 GB to 1,016,500 kB.

prompt: Benchmarked on 100,000 lines, `keep.Load` with no hint did 200,033 allocations and 53,802,259 B per run; with the exact hint, 200,003 allocations and 20,523,557 B. How do thirty allocations account for 33 MB?
hint: The heap profile charged three quarters of all bytes to `keep.Load` itself.

choices.text: The thirty were the ever-larger arrays `append` allocated and copied into
choices.why: Right. Past 256 elements each new array is about a quarter larger than the last, so building 100,000 entries takes some thirty arrays, and the bytes are in them.

choices.text: `B/op` includes the time spent copying, converted to bytes
choices.why: `B/op` is bytes allocated and nothing else. The copying shows up in `ns/op`, which fell by more than half.

choices.text: The hint stopped `strings.Fields` from allocating its slice
choices.why: The hint only sizes the slice of entries. The two allocations a line, from `Text` and `Fields`, are the 200,000 both runs share.

choices.text: The benchmark measured noise: allocations vary from run to run
choices.why: Allocation counts do not depend on how busy the machine is; both numbers come out the same on every run.

prompt: A service records its heap size on every request. Why should it read `runtime/metrics` and not call `runtime.ReadMemStats`?
hint: Look at the third line of `ReadMemStats`'s body.

choices.text: `ReadMemStats` returns numbers from the last collection
choices.why: Its documentation says the opposite: up to date as of the call, unlike a heap profile.

choices.text: `ReadMemStats` allocates a new struct on every call
choices.why: The benchmark showed 0 B/op for both. The cost is elsewhere.

choices.text: `ReadMemStats` stops the world for every call
choices.why: Right. It calls `stopTheWorld`, and the benchmark took 11,398 ns per call against 338.8 for `metrics.Read`, with every goroutine halted for part of it.

choices.text: `runtime/metrics` is the only one that reports heap sizes
choices.why: `MemStats` reports heap sizes too, `HeapAlloc` and `HeapSys` among them, as the `go` course used.

prompt: Inside a benchmark, calling `b.___()` makes that benchmark print `B/op` and `allocs/op` even when `go test` runs without `-benchmem`.
hint: A method of `testing.B`, named for what it does.

prompt: `keep.WriteEntry` keeps `*[]byte` values in its `sync.Pool`, not `[]byte`. What does the pointer save?
hint: `~/mem-pool` printed one number for each kind.

choices.text: A pointer stops two goroutines receiving the same buffer
choices.why: The pool never hands one item to two callers at once, whatever its type. The difference is in what `Put` costs.

choices.text: An allocation on every `Put`
choices.why: Right. `Put` takes an `any`, and a slice's three words have to be copied to the heap to become one: 1 allocation per round trip against 0 for a pointer.

choices.text: A pointer survives two collections in the pool, a slice only one
choices.why: What the pool keeps across collections does not depend on the type; the buffer in `~/mem-pool` was a pointer and was gone after two.

choices.text: The capacity of a `[]byte` is lost when it is stored in an interface
choices.why: A slice keeps its length and capacity in an interface; `b[:0]` came back with room for 64 bytes. It is just more expensive to put there.

prompt: A function reads lines with one reused buffer, the way `keep.Write` does, and passes each line to a callback that does `saved = append(saved, line)`. The tests check a single line and pass. What happens in production?
hint: Who owns the bytes after the callback returns?

choices.text: Every saved line shows the last line's bytes
choices.why: Right. Each element of `saved` is a slice of the same array, which the next line overwrites. It is the ownership rule `io.Writer` states as 'must not retain p', broken by a callback.

choices.text: Each `append` copies the bytes, so nothing goes wrong
choices.why: `append(saved, line)` copies the slice header, not the bytes it points at. That is how slices share arrays.

choices.text: The buffer escapes and the reuse silently stops
choices.why: Escaping decides where the buffer lives, not whether the loop reuses it. The loop still writes into the one array.

choices.text: The race detector reports it the first time it runs
choices.why: With one goroutine there is no race to detect; the bug is aliasing, and it is silent.

prompt: Put in order what happened to the buffer in `~/mem-pool` when it ran with `GOMAXPROCS=1`, from the first step to the last.
hint: The pool has two tiers, and each collection moves things one tier along.
items: `Put` stores the buffer in the pool
a collection moves it to the second tier
a second collection drops it from the pool
`Get` calls `New`, which makes a fresh buffer

prompt: A server parses nested data from clients with a recursive function and no depth limit. Somebody sends input nested ten million levels deep. What happens?
hint: Recall what `-max` showed, and what the default ceiling is.

choices.text: The request's goroutine panics, and the handler's `recover` returns an error
choices.why: A stack overflow is a fatal error, not a panic: `recover` never sees it.

choices.text: The process exits with `fatal error: stack overflow` near 1 GB
choices.why: Right. The runtime doubles the goroutine's stack until the 1,000,000,000-byte ceiling and then ends every goroutine with it, other clients' requests included. Only a depth limit in the parser prevents it.

choices.text: The stack stops at 8 MiB and only that goroutine is killed
choices.why: 8 MiB is a thread's stack. A goroutine's grows to the 1 GB ceiling, and an overflow takes the whole process down.

choices.text: The runtime moves the deepest frames to the heap and the call completes
choices.why: Frames never move to the heap; the stack is one block, copied whole when it grows.

prompt: `hits count` on two million lines spends about 1% of its run collecting, and every cycle finds 0 MB alive. Which change would make it noticeably faster?
hint: Find where the other 99% of the time goes.

choices.text: `GOGC=400`, so that it collects a quarter as often
choices.why: Collecting less often saves part of the 1%; the run cannot get more than about 1% faster that way.

choices.text: A `GOMEMLIMIT` well above its peak
choices.why: A limit the program never approaches changes nothing at all.

choices.text: Less work and fewer allocations per line, in `Parse` itself
choices.why: Right. The time is in parsing two million lines, two allocations each; lesson 13 removed one of the two and the benchmark ran about twice as fast. No collector setting reaches that.

choices.text: A `sync.Pool` for the maps in `Summary`
choices.why: There are two maps per run, made once. Pooling them saves two allocations out of four million.

prompt: Match each situation to the change the lesson's measurements support.
hint: Read `#%` and the live heap before touching anything.

pairs.left: a CLI at 1% `#%` with almost nothing alive
a program alone in a container with a hard memory limit
pairs.right: set `GOMEMLIMIT` a margin below the container's limit

pairs.left: memory to spare, processors busy, `#%` high
a peak that jumps around whatever `GOGC` says
pairs.right: preallocate the slice the program grows
